aide.start.title: Getting started
aide.start.summary: The full cycle of an edition: collect, build, solve, publish, follow up.
aide.start.intro: The application assigns staff to seats. A seat is a place to fill on a stand during a time slot: the solver invents none of them, it only chooses who occupies the ones your stands and time slots already describe. What used to be settled in the layout of the spreadsheet is therefore settled upstream, in the data entry.
aide.start.classeur: Three things change the method compared to a spreadsheet. The legal framework is checked continuously, not on proof-reading. A late change is replayed by an incremental re-plan, which leaves everything still valid untouched. And the published schedule is dated: the application knows who received which version, and who has not read it yet.
aide.start.step1: 1. Pick or create the edition: everything else belongs to it, and nothing travels from one edition to another.
aide.start.step2: 2. Enter the reference data: game categories, locations, stands, staff, time slots. Staff can also come in one go through the CSV import, if your volunteers already arrive in a spreadsheet; a YAML scenario or an SQL dump replaces the whole step. An entry that looks doubtful but holds is saved with a warning to read, never silently refused.
aide.start.step3: 3. Open the availability collection with the “notify” box ticked: it sends everyone the link to their espace, where they declare from their phone the days they cannot come and the games they would like to run. The staff records must therefore already exist; and if you open the collection before entering the time slots, the espace offers no day to tick — only wishes can be declared.
aide.start.step4: 4. Apply or reject the declarations you receive, then close the collection: applying writes the whole proposal onto the animateur's record.
aide.start.step5: 5. Check the stand opening schedule, then the staffing needs: both screens answer without any solve having run.
aide.start.step6: 6. If days are described by a single opening span, generate the slicing into shifts.
aide.start.step7: 7. Run a short solve, read the Problems page, fix — then run again with a long duration.
aide.start.step8: 8. Publish: only the people whose schedule changed receive a message, with the link to their espace. It is also the only moment subscribed calendars move — until you publish, they show the previous version.
aide.start.step9: 9. Follow the acknowledgements on the Staff page, and enable the nightly sends on the Settings page so the silent ones get one reminder — one.
aide.start.step10: 10. Check that the swap fair is open — it is by default — so swaps get negotiated between animateurs, close it once the schedule is frozen. On the day itself, the D-day mode takes over.
aide.start.guichets: Two counters are opened and closed by hand, and they are the only places where an animateur writes anything: the availability collection (Availability page) before the build, the swap fair (Swaps page) after publication. Each also accepts a dated period, but the switch stays in charge — a period entered never opens a closed counter. The collection stays closed until you open it; the fair, on the other hand, is open by default.
aide.start.iterate: The solving steps repeat: a first short solve is there to reveal what is blocking, not to produce the final schedule. Change one thing at a time between two attempts, or nothing is comparable any more.
aide.start.theme: Top right, a button cycles the display through three settings: automatic, light and dark. "Automatic" follows your computer's or phone's own setting — which is why the application may turn dark by itself in the evening. Explicitly picking "light" or "dark" pins the display: this browser remembers it and stops changing its mind.
aide.editions.title: Editions and alternate plans
aide.editions.summary: The edition is the only variant carrier: a heat-wave plan is a duplicated edition, not a parallel grid.
aide.editions.def.edition: One edition of the event — or one plan variant — with its own stands, staff, time slots, parameters and solved schedule. Nothing leaks between editions: “Year 2025” stays readable while “Year 2026” is being prepared, and “2026 heat wave” lives beside “2026” without touching it. The edition you are browsing is per browser tab, and recalled by the banner at the top.
aide.data.title: Reference data
aide.data.summary: What each reference screen describes, and the most common data-entry traps.
aide.data.def.animateurs: Identity, date of birth, skills per category with a level (beginner / autonomous / lead), and unavailable days. The applicable legal regime (under 16, 16-18, adult) is never entered: it is recomputed at the date of each time slot. Staff are available by default: only enter their absences. The table itself only shows what fits in a cell — identity, majority, manager, number of unavailable days, acknowledgement — and each of those columns sorts, bringing up first what is left to do: managers, adults, then the silent ones before the reminded and the confirmed. Appreciation is a list per person: they are read in the consultation record and edited in the form, bulk edit included.
aide.data.def.stands: Categories offered, minimum and maximum number of simultaneous staff, optional adults-only restriction, premium and effort-level flags, and opening hours. Hours are entered as recurring rules (“every day from 10am to noon then from 2pm to closing time”) completed by dated exceptions, which take precedence over the rules for the day they name.
aide.data.def.creneaux: Event day, date, start and end times. This is the time grid the solver fills; a stand's minimum headcount is multiplied by the number of slots it is open on.
aide.data.def.autres: Locations are geolocated places a stand attaches to — they help avoid distant venue changes from one slot to the next. Typologies are the shared vocabulary between a staff member's competences and a stand's games: someone can only run a stand if they master at least one of its typologies. Also designate the “ninja” typology: its holders count as versatile (assignable to any stand), and the solver tries to keep one of them free on every slot — your margin for last-minute absences. Without a designated ninja typology that reserve does not exist and everyone stays within their own competences; it is picked on the Settings page, which warns you when it is missing.
aide.data.bulk: Every reference screen lets you tick several rows to delete or edit them in one go. In a bulk edit, each field means “leave unchanged” until it is filled in: the per-row values of the other fields are preserved. This includes opening hours: a rule shared by several stands (“all closed before 18:00 on a heat-wave evening”) is entered once — tick the stands, “Edit selection”, then add, replace or clear their rules in one go. Time slots, on the other hand, are already shared by every stand: you never create one per stand, the opening hours are what restricts what each stand opens. Before a deletion, single or in bulk, the confirmation states what references the selection: assignments of the saved planning, manual adjustments, locks. It informs, it does not block — no figure ever prevents a deletion.
aide.data.importCsv: If your volunteers arrive in a spreadsheet, the « Animateur CSV import » screen saves retyping everything. Save the sheet as « CSV UTF-8 » (.xlsx is not read, and a file saved in any other encoding is refused: its accents are already lost by the time the file arrives), drop it in, and say which column is which field: a mapping is proposed from the headers, and you correct it. The screen then shows, row by row, what the import would do — accepted, rejected and why, with the line number of the file — and nothing is written until you confirm. By default it adds and updates without deleting anybody, and the file's off days complete the ones already stored rather than erasing them; two checkboxes invert each of those choices. If you tick the full replacement, read the preview's warning before confirming: deleting a fiche also takes that person's availability declaration, their acknowledgement of the published planning and their espace access code. Two refusals surprise on the first attempt and are deliberate: create your timeslots first (without event dates, an imported off day would be invisible in the animateur's espace and then erased), and give every new fiche a birth date (the whole minor / adult regime derives from it). Finally, if two people share a name, add an identifier or e-mail column: the import refuses the row rather than choosing for you.
aide.importCsv.title: Animateur CSV import
aide.importCsv.summary: Reusing the volunteers’ spreadsheet without retyping it: the expected format, the row-by-row preview, and the two refusals that surprise everyone the first time.
aide.importCsv.colonnes: Beyond the name, only one column is really mandatory: the birth date, from which the whole minor / adult regime is derived at each créneau’s date. Competences, wishes and off days may hold several values in one cell, separated by « | » (a semicolon, a comma or a line break inside a quoted cell also work, but never a « / », which a date uses). A competence is written « category » or « category:REFERENT » — without a level it counts as « autonomous ». Dates are read in DD/MM/YYYY as well as in YYYY-MM-DD, and a column left on « — » is not an empty column: the matching field is not touched on the fiches already stored.
aide.importCsv.exemple: The « Download an example file » button of the import screen gives a complete CSV, ready to open in a spreadsheet: the nine columns that are read, filled with the 153 animateurs of the « festival réaliste » demonstration scenario. It is the shortest way to see what a competences cell or an off-days cell should look like. Its off days and its categories are those of that scenario: imported as is into an edition with other dates or other categories, some rows will be rejected — copy its shape, not its content.
aide.data.avertissements: Some entries are saved with a warning: the row really is written, and the message stays on screen until you close it. Four cases, on creation as well as on edit — an off day set outside the event dates (it overlaps no timeslot, so it protects nobody); an off day set on a day of the event that carries no timeslot, a quiet Monday between two weekends for instance: the date is not wrong, but the animateur's espace will not show it and the first availability declaration applied will erase it; a birth date that makes the animateur a minor during the event, the message naming the day they turn 18; a timeslot no stand is open to cover, either entirely or only at its edges. None of these is a refusal: a refusal shows in red and nothing is saved. An edit only reports what it changes: fixing a minor's e-mail does not raise the minority message again, and a bulk edit does not wake up what nobody touched. As long as the edition has no timeslot at all, the event has no dates and these warnings stay silent.
aide.data.ouvertures: Before any solve, open “Stand opening schedule”: the stand × day grid shows what the solver will actually read once rules are expanded and exceptions applied, and reports the three usual entry mistakes — a stand that ends up open on no day at all, a time window outside the day's hours (so with no effect), and an open range too short to be a real shift.
aide.config.title: Configuring the solver
aide.config.summary: The five settings that change how the solver behaves, and which one to touch first.
aide.config.intro: The solver has no “quality level” to set: within the time it is given, it looks for the best schedule according to the active constraints. Settings therefore act either on the time granted, or on the rules to respect.
aide.config.def.duree: The maximum time granted to one solve, set on the Solver page (3 min by default) and shared by every browser. This is the setting that matters most: on a full event, a few minutes are rarely enough to reach a zero hard score. Start short (1 to 3 min) to reveal structural blockers, then move to 15-30 min or more for the final solve.
aide.config.def.legaux: Weekly working-time caps, on the Constraints page: 48h for adults, 35h for minors. These maximums are public-policy ceilings — a higher value is rejected. A lower, more protective value is accepted but makes the problem much harder: it is often the cap, not the head count, that makes a schedule infeasible.
aide.config.def.contraintes: Every rule of the catalogue can be disabled from the Constraints page. Use it to diagnose (“without this rule, does the schedule become feasible?”) far more than to produce: disabling a hard constraint yields a schedule reality will reject. Disabling a soft constraint that measures nothing, however — wishes, when nobody declared any — makes the score readable without changing the result.
aide.adHoc.title: Manual adjustments
aide.adHoc.summary: Force, forbid, pair up: what each type covers exactly, and the edge cases that catch people out.
aide.adHoc.intro: A manual adjustment is an exception you enter against your own data, alongside the catalogue's rules. Three of the four types are enforced at the same level as the legal framework: the solver will never work around them, even if that means returning a schedule in breach. Each one is entered with a reason, which stays readable everywhere the adjustment is quoted.
aide.adHoc.def.indisponibilite: Forbids that person from holding a seat within the chosen scope. Not to be confused with the unavailable days on the staff member's own record, which cover a whole day: here you can target a specific time slot, a specific stand, or both.
aide.adHoc.def.affectation: Requires at least one seat of the scope to be held by that person. Careful: if you name several staff members, the adjustment is satisfied as soon as one of them holds the seat — it means "any one of these", never "all of them". To require two people, enter two adjustments.
aide.adHoc.def.incompatibilite: Forbids two people from working the same time slot. It applies to the time slot, not to the stand: two different stands at the same hour are just as forbidden. Restricting the adjustment to one stand therefore only relaxes it within that stand. Only the first two staff members of the list count: for three people who must not cross paths, enter the three pairs.
aide.adHoc.def.affinite: The only type that is not a hard rule: a plain preference, rewarded whenever both people hold a seat on the same stand at the same time slot. It forces nothing — making it hard would turn it into a forced assignment in disguise, colliding with load balancing and with everyone's own availability.
aide.adHoc.perimetre: The time slot and the stand are optional, and leaving them empty means "everywhere": a forced unavailability with no scope keeps the person out of the whole event. An adjustment keeps the id of the time slot it targets — if that slot is deleted or regenerated by a slicing, the Scope column reads "deleted time slot" and the adjustment no longer applies to anything. After a slicing, check the ones that targeted a slot.
aide.adHoc.contradictions: Two adjustments that cannot both hold are refused when saved, with a message naming both — rather than a schedule declared infeasible minutes later, with nothing pointing at the cause. Four situations are refused:
aide.adHoc.refus1: the same pair declared both incompatible and in affinity;
aide.adHoc.refus2: a forced assignment whose whole scope is covered by a forced unavailability targeting every staff member it names;
aide.adHoc.refus3: two forced assignments pinning the same person onto scopes that overlap in time — nobody holds two seats at the same hour;
aide.adHoc.refus4: two forced assignments placing two people declared incompatible on one time slot.
aide.adHoc.limites: The check only refuses what is certainly impossible: an adjustment refused by mistake would cost you a legitimate entry, with no way around it. So the following deliberately go through: a forced assignment naming two staff members when only one of them is unavailable (the other can satisfy it), an unavailability narrower than the forced scope (the seat can land elsewhere within it), and two forced assignments on the same time slot of which only one names a stand (a single seat satisfies both). Those combinations are not refused, but they can still lead to a schedule in breach: the solve is what settles them.
aide.adHoc.chevauchement: Overlap is computed on the time slot's hours as entered. A stand closure can narrow the range a seat actually covers: two forced assignments on overlapping slots, but on two stands closed at complementary hours, will therefore be refused although the solver could have placed them. The scope of an adjustment is what you typed; in that case, target slots that do not overlap.
aide.adHoc.modifier: Editing an adjustment means saving it again under its own id: the new version replaces the previous one, and that case is never refused as a contradiction with itself. An adjustment recorded before this check existed, or imported, can however survive: the Problems page then reports it as a blocking cause, and the adjustments screen flags the rows concerned. Nothing else would point at them.
aide.adHoc.import: On a scenario import, the file's manual adjustments replace the edition's as a block: a file carrying none installs none. What preserves them across a round-trip is the export, which writes the section whenever the edition holds any. A file whose adjustments contradict each other is refused whole, writing nothing.
aide.adHoc.apres: When a solve still ends in breach, the Problems page names the adjustments the solver could not honour, one by one, with how many violations each accounts for — that is what tells "the solver can't do it" apart from "these three exceptions need arbitrating".
aide.config.def.adhoc: Case-by-case exceptions entered with a traced reason: forced unavailability, incompatibility between two staff members, forced assignment. All three are treated at the same level as hard constraints, so never silently bypassed — and each one takes options away from the solver. A badly entered adjustment blocks a schedule just as surely as a lack of staff. See the « Manual adjustments » section for what each type covers exactly.
aide.config.def.verrouillages: Freeze a staff member, a stand, a day or a time slot so the next solve leaves it alone and optimises the rest. Useful to pin down a validated part of the schedule. An unfilled seat is never frozen, and frozen seats keep being evaluated: a lock can therefore leave a warning visible rather than hide a problem.
aide.config.def.decoupage: For a “continuous” scenario, the slicing turns a day's opening amplitude into real working shifts: target, minimum and maximum shift length, handover overlap, meal-break windows and duration, and the coverage strategy during the break (close the stand, add a relief seat, or run at reduced staffing). These settings are edited on the Settings page; the preview and the generation are launched from the Timeslots page, because the slicing replaces the edition's timeslots in place — to re-slice with other settings, re-import the source scenario. These settings determine the number of seats to fill: changing them changes the problem size far more than any solver knob.
aide.config.lock: Only one solve runs at a time for the whole server — possibly started from another machine or another browser; the toolbar monitor says which one, on which edition and for how long. The run works on the edition it was started from: only that one is locked for data entry and imports. Switching to another edition lets you keep entering data or importing a scenario there while the solve runs.
aide.results.title: Reading and interpreting the results
aide.results.summary: The score, the feasibility banner, the Problems page: what each one says, and which to believe.
aide.results.score: A solve returns a three-part score, of the form “0hard / -6675medium / -120soft”. The parts never compensate for one another: the solver always prefers a schedule that is better on hard, whatever the price paid in medium and soft.
aide.results.courbe: While a solve runs, the Solver page plots those three parts live, each in its own box — a hard score of -36 and a soft score of -400,000 cannot be compared on a single axis. The top of a box is zero: a curve that flattens against it means “nothing left to fix at that level”. That is what tells you when to stop: hard at zero for several minutes and soft no longer moving means the solve has plateaued, and the “Stop solver” button costs you nothing — a stopped solver still saves and analyses what it found. Only the solve currently running is plotted: no history of past solves is kept. If the charts are taking up room for nothing — you launched a fifteen-minute solve and went to do something else — “Shrink the chart” replaces them with a line of scores, and the screen remembers it on your next visit. Shrinking interrupts nothing: reopening shows the solve from its very beginning.
aide.results.def.hard: The only part to look at first. At zero, the schedule is valid: every seat is filled, no unavailability is broken, no skill is missing, nothing overlaps, and the whole legal framework is respected. Negative, the schedule cannot be used as is, whatever the rest of the score says.
aide.results.def.medium: What must be respected as far as possible and reported otherwise — a lead per stand, workload balancing, supervision of minors. A very negative medium does not invalidate the schedule; it points to degraded comfort.
aide.results.def.soft: What separates two valid schedules: stand rotation, mixing skill levels, fair sharing of demanding time slots. Never optimise it before the hard score is zero.
aide.results.mediumFloor: Beware of medium points that measure nothing: a constraint penalising every seat for lack of data — no wish declared, no staff member at lead level — produces a constant floor, sometimes more than 80% of the total. Compare scores between two solves of the same data set, not absolute values.
aide.results.previousPlan: Re-solving an edition that already holds a good schedule can make it worse: the solver starts over and is not bound to do as well again. The Solver page therefore shows the score from before next to the one from after, and flags a solve that scored lower — a hard score still at zero does not mean nothing was lost, the gap shows on the medium. A “Go back to the previous plan” button then puts the earlier schedule back. Do not wait: that safety net is an automatic snapshot, and only the last five are kept per edition.
aide.results.instantanes: Only one schedule is stored at a time, and every solve overwrites the previous one: the Snapshots page is what keeps the others. A capture is taken there automatically before each solve — that is the net “Go back to the previous plan” uses. A plan you want to keep beyond the last five is set aside explicitly, with a label: that one is never purged, and serves as the term of comparison in the A/B comparator. The “Restore this plan” button is disabled while a solve runs: the solve would overwrite the plan just put back when it completes.
aide.results.def.faisabilite: A capacity estimate computed without solving, shown at the top of the Solver and Constraints pages. It names the time slots and stands at fault. It is optimistic: it ignores the slicing into shifts and the legal framework for minors, so it can call “feasible” a schedule the solver will not bring to zero. The converse does not happen: if it reports a lack of capacity, that lack is real.
aide.results.def.problemes: The complete, ranked list of causes, where the banner only shows the most severe ones. It mixes two sources: structural infeasibility causes, computed without any solve (insufficient capacity on a time slice, a typology nobody masters, an adults-only stand with no adult available…) — visible as soon as the data is entered, before any solve — and the failing rules of the last analysis, with their match counts. Each row is sorted by severity and points to the screen where to fix it. It is the first screen to open when a solve does not reach zero, and a good reflex even before launching the first one.
aide.results.def.contraintes: The catalogue of rules, each with its level, its enabled/disabled state and the result of the last analysis: how many times it is violated, and the detail of those violations. This is what turns “-14 hard” into “fourteen unfilled seats on that stand”.
aide.results.def.pourquoiLui: Clicking an assigned staff member, in the daily calendar or the assignment calendar, explains that specific assignment: the rules respected or violated for this seat. On demand, the screen also searches for who could take over, and offers only the replacements that hold — those introducing no hard violation — each with its effect on the score and the rules it clears. The search is bounded: it states how many candidates it evaluated and whether it stopped at the cap, because a short list is no proof that nothing else exists. “Apply” puts the replacement into the schedule.
aide.tuning.title: Tuning the configuration
aide.tuning.summary: Symptom by symptom: what to change, and in which order.
aide.tuning.order: Always tune in this order: the data first, then the solving duration, and only last the constraints. Disabling a rule is a diagnostic tool, not a production method.
aide.tuning.def.postesVides: Check the Staffing needs page first: if the head count entered is below the estimated minimum, staff are missing, not computing time. Otherwise, look at which time slots are involved on the Problems page — it is often a handful of peak time slots, a stand left open by mistake, or a category almost nobody masters.
aide.tuning.term.plateau: The hard score stalls a few units short of zero
aide.tuning.def.plateau: This is the typical case where a longer solving duration pays off: double it and run again. If two long solves stop at exactly the same score, time is no longer the issue — the structure is. Identify the failing rule on the Constraints page and go through its violations one by one.
aide.tuning.def.legal: Weekly caps and rest between days are clashing with the slicing. Revisit the slicing parameters (shorter shifts, overlap, coverage strategy during the break) rather than the legal caps, which cannot be raised. A cap deliberately lowered below the legal maximum is often the real culprit.
aide.tuning.def.mineurs: The rules for minors are stricter and depend on their age at the date of the time slot: no night work, shorter daily span, longer breaks, two consecutive rest days, mandatory supervision by an adult. Check the dates of birth entered and how many adults are available on late time slots.
aide.tuning.term.adhoc: The schedule became infeasible after a change
aide.tuning.def.adhoc: Look at the manual adjustments and planning locks added since the last successful solve: they carry the weight of a hard constraint. Temporarily delete the latest addition and run again to confirm. When two adjustments plainly contradict each other, the Problems page names them with no solve needed.
aide.tuning.term.mediumEleve: The medium or soft score looks huge
aide.tuning.def.mediumEleve: First check it is not a floor caused by missing data (wishes, lead level). Enriching staff skills and wishes improves these parts far more than any solver setting.
aide.tuning.method: Change only one thing between two solves, and always run with the same duration so the scores stay comparable. The seat count and volumetry shown at the top of the Solver page let you check that a data change had the expected effect, before even running a new solve.
aide.views.title: Browsing the schedule
aide.views.summary: Each view answers a different question; picking the right one saves time.
aide.views.def.calendar: A monthly view with filters by staff member and by stand, and the detail of assignments when a day is clicked. To get your bearings across the whole event.
aide.views.def.day: One day, stand by stand and time slot by time slot. To check a specific day or prepare a manual fix.
aide.views.def.heatmap: Day crossed with the stand (seats filled out of seats required: coverage gaps) or with the staff member (seats per day: overloads). To spot an imbalance at a glance.
aide.views.def.timeline: One person's schedule: stands to cover, daily span, shifts and the breaks between them. This is the view to send to the person concerned, exportable as PDF or ICS.
aide.views.def.hours: Hours worked per staff member on one side, the estimated minimum head count to recruit on the other. The latter is computed before any solve, from stands and time slots alone. It also reads game category by game category, at the bottom of the page: a category whose minimum exceeds the number of staff members declaring it is the bottleneck — what is missing there is not staff in general, but staff skilled on that game. Two rules keep that reading honest: a seat counts for a category only when its stand offers that one alone, and a versatile staff member only counts as a specialist in the skills they declared — everywhere else they show up apart, as backup available for any category but for one seat at a time.
aide.exchange.title: Imports, exports and tools
aide.exchange.summary: Getting data in, getting schedules out, and diagnosing the rest.
aide.exchange.item.scenario: Importing a YAML scenario from your machine: the quickest way to fill an empty edition. An invalid file yields a detailed notification rather than a partial import.
aide.exchange.item.csvAnimateurs: Animateur CSV import: reusing the volunteers' spreadsheet without retyping it, with a row-by-row preview before anything is written. The expected format has a section of its own in this guide.
aide.exchange.item.sql: Exporting and importing a full SQL dump, to duplicate or restore an entire data set.
aide.exchange.item.pdfIcs: Exporting one staff member's schedule as PDF or ICS (importable into Google Calendar, Apple Calendar or Outlook), one at a time or as a ZIP archive for everyone. An ICS file is a snapshot: it will not move again. For a calendar that follows republications, what is needed is the staff area's subscription — see “Schedule swap fair”.
aide.exchange.item.yamlValidator: YAML validator (on the Debug page): checks a scenario file without importing anything, to fix it before touching the data.
aide.exchange.item.notifications: Notifications: the history of events — solve completed, import, error. An unread alert is flagged in the navigation.
aide.exchange.item.debug: Debug: the raw state returned by the server, useful to report a problem precisely.
aide.exchange.item.sauvegarde: Nightly backup (Settings page): the whole database is copied to the server's disk every night, and the screen says where the copies go, which ones exist and whether the last one went through. It is not downloadable — it carries everyone's name, birth date and address — and restoring is an operator's task on the server, not a button.
staffing.pauseBound.label: Peak with legal break: {$INTERPOLATION}
staffing.pauseBound.description: — the same peak, each vacation extended by the {$INTERPOLATION} minutes of break required between two vacations of the same person. This is the exact number of distinct staff members the busiest day requires: no solving duration will ever go below it.
staffing.competence.title: Bottleneck per skill
staffing.competence.description: The same bounds, game category by game category: the one whose bound exceeds its specialists is the bottleneck. A versatile staff member counts as backup, never as a specialist. The attribution rules are spelled out on the Help page.
staffing.competence.empty: No seat belongs to a single game category: nothing to break down per skill for now.
staffing.competence.noAnimateurs: No staff member entered yet: the need cannot be computed at all, let alone the bottleneck per skill. Fill in the staff list first.
staffing.competence.noBottleneck: No bottleneck: every category holds at least as many specialists as its bound.
staffing.competence.noBottleneckWithRese: No bottleneck: every category holds at least as many specialists as its bound, and {$reserve} versatile staff members remain available as backup for any of them.
staffing.competence.absorbable: {$manque} seats more than specialists, added up over the categories below. The {$reserve} versatile staff members can back them up, but each one covers a single seat at a time.
staffing.competence.shortfallWithoutNinj: {$manque} seats more than specialists, added up over the categories below. No game category is marked “versatile” in the referential: there is no backup to draw on to absorb them.
staffing.competence.shortfall: {$manque} seats more than specialists, added up over the categories below, against only {$reserve} versatile staff members as backup: the reserve is thinner than the shortfalls added up.
staffing.competence.shortfallOnReserve: {$manque} seats more than specialists, added up over the categories below, {$renforts} of them on the versatile category itself: since that pool is the backup, nothing can absorb that part of the shortfall.
staffing.competence.unattributed: {$count} seats belong to stands offering several game categories: either pool can hold them, so no category claims them here.
staffing.competence.polyvalentsOnly: {$count} seats belong to stands offering no game category at all: only versatile staff can hold them, so they are counted in the versatile category’s row.
staffing.competence.nobodyEligible: {$count} seats belong to stands offering no game category at all, and no category is marked “versatile”: nobody in the referential is eligible to hold them. Fill in those stands’ game category.
staffing.competence.ninjaTooltip: The versatile category: its holders can hold any stand, but only count as specialists in the skills they declare — everywhere else they are backup.

aide.tuning.term.gelerBloc: Part of the planning is settled and slows the search down
aide.tuning.def.gelerBloc: Some days are bulky and easy — set-up and tear-down typically: many seats, a single typologie, no skill requirement. The solver still spends a share of its moves on them proportional to their seat count. Once a run has staffed them correctly, put a Stand lock on those stands: the seats stay in the planning in full, named and visible everywhere, their hours keep counting towards the legal caps, but the solver stops trying to move them and spends its budget on the hard days. Keep this for diagnosis and large scenarios: the lock freezes those people on those seats, so it is only sound if the frozen assignment is already good — hence the order « solve, check, then lock ». It can be removed at any time from the Locks page.

aide.foire.title: Schedule swap fair (shift swaps)
aide.foire.summary: Staff members propose their shift swaps themselves; nothing is applied without your approval.
aide.foire.intro: Each staff member has a personal area, reached through the link printed on their PDF schedule — no account needed, but an access code sent to the e-mail address on their record is required once per device (the schedule can be downloaded from the area, so a minimum of authentication is due; a staff member without an address must have one added). There they see their up-to-date schedule (with teammates) and can propose swapping one of their slots with a colleague — either by simply giving their slot away, or by also designating the colleague's slot they want back in exchange (“I leave you my Monday, I take your Tuesday”). The colleague they name agrees first, from their own area (the Swaps tab shows them the requests received): a request only reaches the organisation’s Swaps screen once both staff members agree, and a refusal from the colleague closes it with nothing to arbitrate. Every request is prechecked against the hard scheduling rules; an infeasible one is flagged in business words but still sent: you decide.
aide.foire.def.espace: The staff member builds their list of requests (time slot, colleague to swap with, reason) then submits it in one go. When they have nobody in mind — they simply do not want that time slot — “who can replace me?” searches the colleagues an exchange would really work with, in its three forms: a free colleague takes over, a swap on the same time slot, or a trade against a time slot on another day. They pick from the list and the colleague field fills itself. They then follow each request's status — pending, accepted, refused — with your optional comment, and can cancel a request while it is undecided. They can also take their schedule away from the “My schedule” tab: the “Take my schedule with me” band offers first to subscribe their calendar to it, then to download a PDF or an ICS file. The link to their area can be copied (and regenerated, if a PDF leaked) from their record on the Staff page.
aide.foire.def.planPublie: A staff member's space shows the plan they were sent, not the one you are working on: a validated swap, an applied replacement or a fresh solve only move their space once published. Until something has been published on the edition, the spaces stay empty and say so — the application cannot claim to have communicated a schedule it never sent. The first publication therefore concerns everyone. Publishing is refused while a solve runs: it would freeze a plan about to be rewritten.
aide.foire.def.abonnement: From the “Take my schedule with me” band of their espace, a staff member gives their calendar a permanent subscription address instead of downloading an ICS file that goes stale on the next publication. What that calendar re-reads on every sync is the published schedule: “my calendar is not updating” therefore almost always means the change has not been published yet, and never that they must subscribe again. As long as nothing has been published on the edition, the subscription answers an empty calendar rather than an error — a calendar answered with an error drops the subscription without telling anybody. That address is a second credential, separate from the espace link: regenerating a staff member's link from their record does not cut their subscription, and they replace their own subscription address if it leaked, without their espace link changing. You never see it and never have to handle it.
aide.foire.def.ouverture: The switch at the top of the Swaps screen opens or closes the fair for the current edition. Closed, the staff areas turn read-only — the schedule stays visible, downloadable (PDF, ICS) and subscribed calendars keep following it, but no request can be submitted or withdrawn any more, and the refusal is enforced server-side, not merely hidden on screen. You can also bound the fair with a start and an end date, like the availability collection: leave a date empty to leave that side unbounded. The switch stays in charge — a period never opens a closed fair — and the bounds are enforced server-side too. Before the opening date the staff area says “not open yet” and gives the date to come back, rather than “closed”: someone told it is over two weeks too early does not come back.
aide.foire.def.ecran: The pending requests, each with its measured impact on the current schedule: cross swap (both trade places) or simple takeover (the colleague is free on the slot), score effect, hard rules that would break. Accepting applies the swap immediately, exactly as simulated, and locks it on its time slot: a later regeneration will not undo it — regeneration itself stays on the Solver page. Refusing changes nothing; the reason you type is sent to the staff member.
aide.foire.def.connexion: The administration is protected by the admin account; only the staff areas remain reachable through their personal link. If mailing is configured, you are notified by email at every submission. The staff member, however, learns the fate of their requests at the next publication, along with the schedule that carries it: accepting a swap changes the working plan, not yet the one they received.
aide.foire.def.envoi: The "Publish" button on the Solver page (next to the global schedule export) carries its own count: “Publish — 3 people concerned”. It only writes to the staff members whose schedule changed since the last publication, and the message says what changes for each of them — the same list you review on screen before confirming. A correction that moves nobody therefore triggers no send at all, and ten corrections in a row do not make ten e-mails: they fill a queue you empty once you are done. The report names the staff members without an e-mail address and the failed sends; the Staff timeline page can resend one of them the published plan. With a large team the send takes tens of seconds: the screen says so and disables the button while it goes out, one send at a time — no need to click again.
aide.editions.variante: To prepare an alternate plan (heat wave, fallback), duplicate the edition: the copy carries stands, hours, staff and their current unavailabilities — but neither the assignments nor the espace tokens (each edition mints its own, a link always designates exactly one edition). Then apply the delta in the copy (the bulk hours editor is made for it), launch the solve, and switch editions when the morning comes.

mcp.connexion.subtitle: The application exposes an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server letting an AI assistant — Claude, an IDE, an agent — read and drive the planning in natural language: list the referentials, launch a solve, explain a score.
mcp.connexion.endpoint: The entry point is {$START_TAG_CODE}{$INTERPOLATION}/mcp{$CLOSE_TAG_CODE} (streamable HTTP transport). Every request must present the shared API key in the {$START_TAG_CODE}{$INTERPOLATION_1}{$CLOSE_TAG_CODE} header — the value of the server variable {$START_TAG_CODE}PLANNING_MCP_API_KEY{$CLOSE_TAG_CODE}; as long as it is not configured server-side, the MCP answers 401 to everyone.

mcp.pangolin.title: Pangolin access proxy detected
mcp.pangolin.warning: This instance answers behind a Pangolin access proxy: on top of the API key, every MCP request must present a proxy access token, to be created in Pangolin then configured in the client.
mcp.pangolin.headers: The standard headers Pangolin expects are {$START_TAG_CODE}P-Access-Token-Id{$CLOSE_TAG_CODE} (the token id) and {$START_TAG_CODE}P-Access-Token{$CLOSE_TAG_CODE} (the token itself) — the configuration above already includes them. A client unable to add headers can pass the token as a query string: {$START_TAG_CODE}?p_token=<id>.<token>{$CLOSE_TAG_CODE}.
mcp.pangolin.authorization: Do use the dedicated {$START_TAG_CODE}X-MCP-Api-Key{$CLOSE_TAG_CODE} header for the API key rather than {$START_TAG_CODE}Authorization: Bearer{$CLOSE_TAG_CODE}: an access proxy frequently consumes {$START_TAG_CODE}Authorization{$CLOSE_TAG_CODE} for its own sake, and the key would never reach the application.
mcp.pangolin.jeton.revele: The Pangolin token configured server-side has been revealed: the configuration above contains its real value rather than a placeholder.

Otherwise, its value has to be pasted into the configuration by hand.

aide.rappels.title: Acknowledgements and automatic reminders
aide.rappels.summary: Know who has read their schedule, and let the application chase the others — once.
aide.rappels.intro: Once the schedule is published, every staff member sees an “I have read it and I will be there” button in their space. The “Acknowledgement” column of the Staff page gives you the answer back, and the table's quick filter accepts “confirmed”, “reminded” or “silent” like any other word.
aide.rappels.def.statuts: “Silent”: nothing came back. “Confirmed”: the button was clicked, the date shows on hover. “Reminded”: the automatic reminder went out and is still unanswered. Someone with no assignment in the published schedule shows “—”: they are not silent, nobody asked them anything, and they do not count among the people to chase.
aide.rappels.def.republication: A new publication only asks again those whose schedule really changed. Someone merely told that a swap was decided reads the same days as before: asking again would turn the button into a reflex rather than an answer.
aide.rappels.term.activation: Enable the edition, on the Settings page
aide.rappels.def.activation: Nightly sends stay off until you enable them, edition by edition. That is deliberate and it is the only safeguard: a past edition holds the same staff, and nothing else tells this year's volunteers from last year's. Duplicating an edition does not copy this setting.
aide.rappels.def.delais: The sending time of the day-before reminder (23:00 at the latest: the job runs once an hour, and a reminder set later would never go out), the silence tolerated after a publication before following up, and the age of a swap request that triggers an alert. All three are set per edition on the Settings page.
aide.rappels.def.rappel: The evening before, every staff member assigned the next day receives the list of their slots. It is taken from the published schedule, never from the working plan: nobody is reminded about a slot you did not communicate to them. Someone with no e-mail address is skipped, and reported by name on the Notifications page — those are the people to reach out to by hand.
aide.rappels.def.relance: Past the delay, the silent ones receive a confirmation reminder and move to “Reminded”. They will not get another: chasing someone every evening does not make them answer faster, it makes them filter your messages. The last few are yours to take over.
aide.rappels.def.echanges: A request awaiting your decision for longer than the set delay surfaces on the Notifications page, once and only once — even as it keeps ageing. The age is counted from the colleague's agreement: a request still awaiting their answer is not waiting on you.
aide.rappels.silence: “I did not receive anything” almost always has the same cause: the edition was not enabled. Next come a schedule never published, then records with no e-mail address. These alerts are closed by dealing with what they report, not by clearing them.
espace.aide.confirmer.question: What does “I have read it and I will be there” mean?
espace.aide.confirmer.resume: One click telling the organisation you have seen your schedule. One is enough.
espace.aide.confirmer.pourquoi: The button appears as soon as your schedule has been published. It asks for nothing but a click: the organisation then knows you are aware, and does not have to chase you. Without an answer after a few days, an automatic reminder is sent to you — once only.
espace.aide.confirmer.deuxFois: Clicking twice changes nothing: the first date is the one kept, and the button then gives way to “Attendance confirmed on…”.
espace.aide.confirmer.republication: If the organisation publishes a new version and your days change, you are asked again — and only you. When nothing moved for you, your confirmation stands: you will not be made to reconfirm an identical schedule.
espace.aide.confirmer.probleme: Confirming is not an irrevocable commitment, and it is not the right place to report a problem either. If a slot does not work, use the Swaps tab or contact the organisation.
espace.aide.veille.question: Will I get a reminder before the event?
espace.aide.veille.resume: The evening before, an e-mail lists your assignments for the next day.
espace.aide.veille.contenu: If the organisation enabled reminders, the evening before you receive the list of your slots for the next day: time and stand, nothing more. It is exactly what this page already shows — a reminder never announces a change to you, it repeats what was communicated.
espace.aide.veille.absence: No reminder received? Three possible reasons: your record carries no e-mail address, the organisation did not enable reminders, or you are not assigned anywhere that day. In every case, this page remains the reference.
animateurs.confirmation.aide:
What the staff member answered to the schedule that was sent to them.

• Confirmed: they clicked “I have read it and I will be there”. The date shows on hover.
• Reminded: an automatic message has already been sent to them. There will not be another — the last silent ones are yours to chase by hand.
• Silent: nothing came back.
• —: this person has no assignment in the published schedule. That is not silence, nobody asked them anything.

Republishing only sends back to “silent” the people whose schedule really changed: those whose days did not move keep their confirmation.

aide.contact.title: Contact and support
aide.contact.summary: A question, a blocker, a business error: who to reach and how.
aide.contact.mail: For a usage question, a doubt about a result or some guidance, write to planning@sylvain.dev — attach a screenshot if possible and the version shown at the bottom of the Debug page.
aide.contact.issue: For a reproducible business error (a wrong score, a violated constraint, an incorrect export), open a problem report on GitHub: the form guides the description. Careful, GitHub is public: put no personal information there — designate people by their staff id (visible on the Staff page), never by name. Personal data goes through the e-mail above.
aide.data.def.familles: When the slicing is generated with several staggered relay grids, every shift exists in several variants with slightly shifted cut points: the “families” (Family column of the Timeslots page). Each stand is attached to a single family, so stands do not all change teams at the same instant — without staggering, every handover would empty the whole event at once. Identical-looking timeslots belonging to different families are therefore not duplicates. On the needs side, a stand only generates seats on the timeslots of its own family: the total staffing need does not multiply with the number of families, it spreads out — the Staffing need page accounts for it.

aide.config.file: While a run is under way, the two launch buttons become “Plan the solve” and “Plan the replanning”: the task is queued and starts by itself as soon as the previous one finishes. That is the gesture for chaining two editions without waiting in front of the screen — prepare the next one, plan its run, close the screen. A waiting task locks nothing, and it reads its edition as it will be when it starts: a correction made in the meantime is taken into account. The queue is shown under the buttons, a line can be removed from it until it starts, and planning the same task twice (same edition, same run) is refused — the classic double-click. Planning a fresh solve of the edition currently being solved stays allowed: the run under way started before your last corrections and cannot account for them. The queue lives in memory: restarting the server empties it.
solver.diffusion.title: Sharing the schedule
solver.diffusion.hint: What leaves the application once the schedule is good enough: the documents to print or archive, and publishing the schedule. Publishing sends their up-to-date schedule to the people whose own schedule changed since last time, and only to them, spelling out what changed — and that published plan is what every staff member sees in their space. These actions read the plan saved for the edition on screen; they are only unavailable while a solve runs on that edition, since it is busy rewriting it. A solve started on another edition does not block them.

Using it — as an administrator or from an animateur's personal space — constitutes acceptance of these terms.
cgu.aideDecision.title: The tool assists the decision, it does not make it
cgu.aideDecision.texte: The application computes schedule proposals from the data entered: stands, timeslots, availability, skills, and the configured working-time rules. That computation is a {$START_TAG_STRONG}decision aid{$CLOSE_TAG_STRONG}. It amounts to neither legal validation, nor certification of compliance, nor any commitment as to whether a schedule is actually workable.

cgu.aideDecision.limites: The results depend entirely on the accuracy of the data entered and the parameters chosen. A wrong date of birth, an undeclared unavailability or a badly set hourly ceiling produce a schedule the application will deem valid and which will not be.

espace.aide.espace.question: What is this space for?
espace.aide.espace.resume: To read your personal schedule, always up to date, and to request a timeslot swap.
espace.aide.espace.intro: The organisers build the schedule of the event by spreading the staff across the stands, timeslot by timeslot. This space is your personal view of that schedule: your timeslots, and nothing else.
espace.aide.espace.item1: Read your timeslots day by day, with the stand and your teammates.
espace.aide.espace.item2: Take your schedule with you as a PDF or in your phone's calendar.
espace.aide.espace.item3: Request a timeslot swap with a colleague, as long as the schedule fair is open.
espace.aide.espace.item4: Answer the swap requests colleagues send you.
espace.aide.espace.limite: You never change the schedule directly: everything goes through a request the organisers validate.
espace.aide.acces.question: How do I get into my space?
espace.aide.acces.resume: Through your personal link, then a code received by e-mail, asked once per device.
espace.aide.acces.intro: The link the organisers sent you is personal: it points to your schedule and to yours only. The first time you open it on a phone or a computer, a code is sent to the e-mail address the organisation knows. It is valid for 10 minutes.
espace.aide.acces.item1: One code per device: once entered, that device keeps the access, you do not have to start over.
espace.aide.acces.item2: Code not received? Look in your spam folder, then ask for a new one.
espace.aide.acces.item3: Do not forward your link: whoever opens it reaches your schedule.
espace.aide.acces.item4: “This link is no longer valid”: contact the organisers, they will send you a new one.
espace.aide.planning.question: How do I read my schedule?
espace.aide.planning.resume: One card per day; on each line, the hours, the stand and your teammates.
espace.aide.planning.def.horaire: The start and the end of your timeslot. You are expected at the stand at the start time, not at the stand's opening time.
espace.aide.planning.def.stand: The game or the post you run during that timeslot. It can change from one timeslot to the next within the same day.
espace.aide.planning.def.coequipiers: The staff assigned to the same stand, on the same timeslot as you.
espace.aide.planning.repos: Days where you are assigned nowhere still show up, marked “Day off”: a day missing from the list would read as an oversight, a “Day off” day reads as a decision.
espace.aide.planning.maj: The line “Schedule communicated on…” tells how old the version you are reading is. It is the one the organisers sent you: it only changes when they publish again, and you are then told by e-mail what moves for you. Come back to this page before you leave anyway, it is the one that counts.
espace.aide.planning.vide: If nothing shows up, the schedule has not been published yet. There is nothing for you to do.
espace.aide.emporter.question: Can I take my schedule with me?
espace.aide.emporter.resume: Yes — best of all by subscribing to it, so that it keeps itself up to date.
espace.aide.emporter.item0: “Subscribe in my calendar”: your timeslots show up in your calendar and follow every republication. Nothing to redo afterwards.
espace.aide.emporter.item1: “Download as PDF”: your schedule on one page, to print or to keep offline.
espace.aide.emporter.item2: “Download the ICS file”: each timeslot becomes an appointment, poured once into your phone's calendar.
espace.aide.emporter.photo: Both files are a snapshot taken at download time: they do not update on their own when the schedule changes or when a swap is accepted. When in doubt, trust this page rather than the file.
espace.aide.emporter.abonnement: At the top of the "My schedule" page, the "Take my schedule with me" band offers three ways out. The first one, "Subscribe in my calendar", is the one to prefer: given once to your calendar, the address keeps it up to date on its own every time a new version is published.
espace.aide.emporter.abonnementColler: Some applications, Google Calendar first of all, want the address pasted rather than clicked. It is then under "Copy the address, or replace it", in the same band.
espace.aide.emporter.abonnementPrudence: That address is personal: whoever gets it sees your schedule, with no code and no password. Do not publish it on a shared calendar, and if it gets out, the "This address leaked, replace it" button — in the same place — creates a new one, the old one stopping immediately.
espace.aide.echange.question: How do I request a swap?
espace.aide.echange.resume: From “My swaps”, by building a list of requests then submitting it.
espace.aide.echange.step1: Pick the timeslot you want to be freed from.
espace.aide.echange.step2: Pick the colleague to swap with.
espace.aide.echange.step3: If you want one of their timeslots in return, designate it. Without that choice, the swap plays out on yours alone.
espace.aide.echange.step4: Give a reason: this is what the organisers will read to decide.
espace.aide.echange.step5: “Add to the list”, then start over if several timeslots are involved.
espace.aide.echange.step6: “Submit my requests”: nothing leaves before that button.
espace.aide.echange.brouillon: Until you submit, the list is only a draft: the cross removes a request, and nobody has received anything yet.
espace.aide.remplacants.question: I have nobody in mind, what now?
espace.aide.remplacants.resume: The “Who can replace me?” button searches the swaps that hold for you.
espace.aide.remplacants.intro: Once your timeslot is picked, this button goes through your colleagues and only keeps the swaps compatible with the rest of the schedule and with the rest rules. The proposals come in three families:
espace.aide.remplacants.term.libere: Someone frees you from this timeslot
espace.aide.remplacants.def.libere: A colleague takes it over and you are off duty at that moment, with nothing in return.
espace.aide.remplacants.term.dirige: You trade it for another timeslot
espace.aide.remplacants.def.dirige: You leave them yours and take one of theirs, at another moment.
espace.aide.remplacants.term.croise: You swap on that same timeslot
espace.aide.remplacants.def.croise: You stay on duty at the same hours, but on another stand.
espace.aide.remplacants.limite: The list shows the most promising leads, not all of them. And if nothing comes out, you can still propose the swap to someone: the organisers will decide.
espace.aide.suivi.question: What happens to my request?
espace.aide.suivi.resume: It goes through your colleague's agreement, then through the organisers' decision.
espace.aide.suivi.intro: Each request carries a chip saying where it stands:
espace.aide.suivi.def.attenteCible: Your colleague has to agree first.
espace.aide.suivi.def.proposee: The agreement is given; the organisers still have to decide.
espace.aide.suivi.def.acceptee: The swap is done: your schedule has changed, check it.
espace.aide.suivi.def.refusee: The organisers did not keep the swap; your timeslot stays yours.
espace.aide.suivi.def.refuseeCible: The colleague did not want the swap; the request is closed.
espace.aide.suivi.alerte: A box reading “this swap would cause a problem” means the swap hits a rule: rest time too short, hours already taken, a stand expecting you at the same moment… It is a warning, not a refusal, and the request is sent all the same.
espace.aide.suivi.annulation: As long as a request has not been decided, “Cancel this request” withdraws it. And if the organisers attached a comment to their decision, it shows right below.
espace.aide.recues.question: A colleague is asking me for a swap
espace.aide.recues.resume: They are waiting for your agreement: nothing moves until you answer.
espace.aide.recues.intro: Requests addressed to you show at the top of “My swaps”, under “Received requests”. Read the timeslot you are offered to take over and, if there is one, the timeslot taken from you in return.
espace.aide.recues.item1: “I agree” sends the request to the organisers, who decide: your agreement alone is not enough to swap.
espace.aide.recues.item2: “Decline” closes the request, and your colleague is informed.
espace.aide.foire.question: Why can I no longer request anything?
espace.aide.foire.resume: The schedule fair is closed: the space becomes read-only.
espace.aide.foire.intro: The schedule fair is the period during which the organisers accept swaps. Once it is closed — because the schedule is frozen, or because the event has started — you keep access to your schedule and to the history of your requests, but you can no longer propose, agree to or cancel any.
espace.aide.foire.suite: If something comes up after the closing, tell the organisers directly: they can still act, this space cannot.
espace.aide.contact.question: A mistake, a question?
espace.aide.contact.resume: The organisers remain your contact; this space does not replace a word or a call.
espace.aide.contact.item1: An assignment looks wrong, or an unavailability you announced was not taken into account: report it. Outside a collection period, you cannot correct your own data.
espace.aide.contact.item2: Last-minute impediment: tell them right away, without waiting for a swap request to be validated.
espace.aide.contact.item3: What the application knows about you and what it does with it is described in the privacy policy, in the menu at the top right of the screen.

aide.jourJ.title: Event-day mode
aide.jourJ.summary: Under development. Somebody has not shown up: mark them absent, find a replacement, apply — without starting a solve.
aide.jourJ.intro: Every other screen works ahead of the event. This one is built for the day itself, standing in an aisle, on a phone: few taps, large targets, and the three steps in the order the gesture actually goes — who is missing, which seats that opens, who can take them.
aide.jourJ.portee: Marking somebody absent declares them unavailable on the remaining time slots of the day, and on those only. A slot counts as remaining until it is over — the one under way is included, since that is precisely the one nobody is standing at. Slots already past are never touched: the person really did hold them, and the schedule must keep saying so.
aide.jourJ.refus: The absence is applied whole or not at all. It is refused, writing nothing, if it contradicts a forced assignment on one of the slots concerned — the message names both adjustments — or if one of the seats to free is locked: lift the lock first.
aide.jourJ.suggestions: For each open seat, the assistant proposes the viable replacements, best first, and proposes none that would break a hard rule. It stops at the first twenty eligible candidates, because each one costs a full analysis of the schedule: the screen always shows how many were evaluated out of how many eligible, so that a shortened list does not read as “there is nobody else”. Applying a suggestion reassigns that one seat, without starting a solve.
aide.jourJ.publication: Nothing is sent to the staff from this screen: their space keeps showing the published schedule until you publish again. The banner recalls how many people are waiting for a change and links to the Publish button on the Solver page — a send to a hundred and fifty people a thumb away inside an emergency screen would cost dearly.
aide.jourJ.trace: Every absence marked here is a recorded manual adjustment, with its reason, its author and its timestamp: it can be found unchanged the next day on the Manual adjustments page. It can be undone slot by slot or as a block — but seats already reassigned do not come back on their own: who holds a seat remains a decision.
dateMock.tooltip: MOCK — today's date is frozen to {$date} on this server. The screens that reason about “now”, the event-day mode first of all, are not showing reality. Click to change or clear that date.
debug.dateDuJour.title: Today's date (mock)
debug.dateDuJour.description: Freezes the date the server treats as “today”, so the event-day mode can be tried outside the period of the event. Only the date is replaced: the time of day stays real, and nothing else is affected — neither the minor/adult status nor the timestamp of what gets recorded. Leave the field empty to return to the machine's clock.
debug.dateDuJour.label: Today's date
debug.dateDuJour.actif: Date frozen: the screens that reason about “now” are not showing reality.
aide.jourJ.mock: This screen only ever talks about today, which makes it hard to explore outside the period of the event. In development only, the Debug page therefore lets you freeze the date the server treats as today; a warning icon then appears in the top bar, on every screen, and its link takes you straight back to the field to change or clear it. On a deployed instance the setting does not exist and the server refuses to set it: the screen always reads the real clock there.
jourJ.resume.vide: No timeslot is scheduled on that day: there is no journée to cover.
aide.jourJ.journee: A journée starts at its first timeslot, not at midnight: a festival begins when the first stand opens. An evening running past midnight is therefore still the same journée, and at one in the morning the screen still shows yesterday's as long as its last timeslot is running. A 22:00-02:00 shift belongs to the evening that opens it, and to that evening alone. When nothing is running — between two journées, or on a date with no timeslot scheduled at all — the screen says so instead of inventing a journée.
jourJ.wip.message: This screen is under development and, unlike the other screens on trial, it acts: marking somebody absent writes real unavailabilities and empties real seats of the saved plan. Its effects are not guaranteed yet — no solve rechecks the whole before the next one you start.
jourJ.wip.marche: marking somebody absent over the remaining timeslots of the day, undoing that absence, and applying a proposed replacement — each of those writes to the saved plan straight away
jourJ.wip.manque: any check of overall consistency without starting a solve, and handing the seats back when an absence is undone
aide.jourJ.essai: This screen is under development, and its effects are not guaranteed yet. It differs from the other screens on trial on one point that matters: it acts. Marking somebody absent writes real unavailabilities and empties real seats of the saved plan, straight away. No solve rechecks the whole in between: overall consistency is only established by the next one you start. Use it knowing that, and start a solve as soon as the situation allows.
bancDeTouche.title: Bench
bancDeTouche.description: For a given timeslot, who is not assigned anywhere — and, for each of them, the rule that would stop them taking the seat under review. Every reason is a constraint the solver actually enforces, shown with its wording from the catalogue: this screen rewrites none of them. All applicable reasons are listed, not just the most blocking one. Read-only: assigning somebody goes through the repair assistant.
bancDeTouche.everyoneOnDuty: Everybody is on duty on this timeslot: the bench is empty.
bancDeTouche.noReason: No rule stands in the way
bancDeTouche.seatTaken: This seat is held by {$animateur} — the question asked is “who could replace them?”.
bancDeTouche.summary: {$available} staff members available out of {$total} off duty on this timeslot
aide.views.def.banc: For one timeslot, who is not assigned anywhere — and, for each of them, the rule that would stop them taking the seat left open: unavailable that day, legal rest, hours cap reached, missing appreciation. All applicable reasons are shown, not just the first one: that is what tells you whether lifting one obstacle would be enough. The view is read-only; to act, go through the repair assistant of the daily calendar. It reads the saved schedule and therefore only offers the timeslots that schedule staffs: a timeslot where no stand is open does not appear, and before any solve has run the screen says so instead of staying blank. It ships on trial, under “Under development”: it may be withdrawn if it proves of no use.
bancDeTouche.noPlan: No saved schedule yet: run a solve so this screen has a plan to question.
bancDeTouche.noSeat: No seat on this timeslot in the saved schedule: no stand is open then, or the timeslot was created after the last solve. Pick a timeslot that carries seats, or run a solve again.
bancDeTouche.essai: This screen ships on trial: it changes nothing and may be withdrawn if it proves of no use. What it shows is accurate, though, since every reason comes from the constraints themselves — tell us whether it helps.
bancDeTouche.wip.marche: the reasons shown are those of the constraints the solver really enforces, read off the saved schedule — what is written there is accurate
bancDeTouche.wip.manque: acting from this screen, and choosing which seat is evaluated when a timeslot has several free ones

aide.views.def.railJour: The same day as the day calendar, but seen person by person: one line per staff member, the shifts placed on the time axis. Gaps, daily spans and back-to-back chains jump out, and the empty lines say who is still available — the ones marked « unavailable » mean the opposite: do not call on that person.
aide.views.def.repos: The other views turned around: not who is where, but who gets a breather. One line per staff member, one column per day of the event, and only three states — working day (with the number of hours), rest day, unavailable. A rest day is a day the person could have worked and the schedule did not assign them to; a day they declared unavailable is not one, they could not be called on. The most strained lines come first: those chaining the most consecutive working days, and those with no free day at all. The « Run » column gives that longest run, and the table footer says how many people rest each day — hence how many are left to call. A red cell flags an assignment placed on a day declared unavailable: an anomaly of the plan, to be fixed.
aide.views.def.graphe: The same data taken from the ground: a location, the stands standing on it, the time slots they are staffed on, who is assigned there. One column per level, click to open the next one. This is the view for whoever knows the site plan better than the list of stands. The last two columns read from the saved schedule and stay empty until a solve has run; the locations and their stands come from the reference data and can be browsed straight away.
aide.views.def.kpi: One line per completed solve, across all editions: score, coverage, spread of hours, number of manual changes, duration. It is the memory of past campaigns — it says whether the current edition is settling better or worse than the previous one, and how many manual fixes it took. Nothing in it is nominative, and the history outlives the deletion of the edition it describes.

espace.aide.dispo.question: How do I say when I cannot come?
espace.aide.dispo.resume: Under “My availability”, as long as the organisation has opened collection.
espace.aide.dispo.intro: Before building the schedule, the organisation opens a period during which everyone says which days they cannot come, and which kinds of games they would like to run. You do it from the “My availability” tab, on your phone: the days of the event show as chips, tap the ones that do not work.
espace.aide.dispo.etape1: Tap every day you cannot come. Days you do not tap mean “I am available”.
espace.aide.dispo.etape2: Pick the kinds of games you would enjoy. A wish is not a guarantee: it is honoured when the schedule allows it.
espace.aide.dispo.etape3: Add a word if your situation does not fit in boxes (“I am leaving on Sunday after lunch”).
espace.aide.dispo.etape4: Send. The form already opens on what the organisation knows about you: you correct, you do not start from scratch.
espace.aide.dispo.item1: What you send is a proposal: the organisation reviews and applies it, or answers you. Nothing is recorded on your record before that.
espace.aide.dispo.item2: You can send a corrected version while collection is open: it replaces the previous one, there are never two pending.
espace.aide.dispo.item3: Your skills are not declared here: they stay decided with the organisation.
espace.aide.dispo.item4: Once collection is closed the tab stays readable but accepts no submission — contact the organisation directly then.
dispo.intro: The unavailable days and wishes animateurs declare themselves from their espace, during the collection window you open. aide.dispo.title: Availability and preference collection
aide.dispo.summary: Animateurs declare their own unavailable days and wishes; you apply them, or not.
aide.dispo.intro: Before building a schedule you need to know who cannot come when. Rather than collecting that outside the application and typing it back in, you open a collection window: every animateur declares from their espace, on their phone, the days they are unavailable and the kinds of games they would like to run. What they send touches nothing: it is a proposal, waiting for your decision on the Availability screen.
aide.dispo.def.fenetre: The “Collection window” panel, at the top of the Availability page, carries the two buttons “Open collection” and “Close collection”. It is closed until you open it — unlike the swap fair, which is open by default. Both dates are optional: they bound the period, the switch stays in charge. Closed, the espace refuses any declaration server-side, not merely on screen; the animateur keeps access to what they declared and to your answers.
aide.dispo.def.prevenir: A checkbox at opening time, never a permanent setting: it sends everyone the link to their espace, straight to the declaration tab. Tick it on the first round; leave it alone when you reopen the window after a correction, or everybody gets a reminder for nothing. The report names those without an e-mail address and the failed sends.
aide.dispo.term.decision: Apply or refuse, as a whole
aide.dispo.def.decision: The screen shows side by side what the animateur declares and what their record says today. Applying writes the whole proposal onto their record, exactly as if you had opened it to edit it — the stored schedule is then flagged as stale, and regenerating stays a separate action from the Solver page. Refusing changes nothing; the reason you type is read by the animateur in their espace. There is deliberately no line-by-line approval: a disagreement is settled with a word, and the animateur sends a corrected version.
aide.dispo.def.remplacement: An animateur correcting themself replaces their pending proposal, they do not stack a second one: you will never have to arbitrate two contradictory versions of the same person, and what reaches you is always the latest. You are e-mailed when a proposal lands on your desk, not on every correction they make to it before you process it.
aide.dispo.def.competences: Skills stay decided with you. A self-declared skill feeds hard rules — who may staff which stand — and the stakes are not those of an unavailability or a wish, which can be caught up. An animateur declaring a day outside the dates of the event, or a game category that does not exist, is refused on submission.
